headline_marked: [[PDF Regex Endpoint]] Skips OCR Entirely for Born-Digital Documents
headline: PDF Regex Endpoint Skips OCR Entirely for Born-Digital Documents
summary: PDF4me's new endpoint bypasses OCR for digitally generated PDFs, directly extracting text via regex for faster, cheaper processing.
details: Many document processing pipelines automatically run Optical Character Recognition (OCR) on all incoming PDFs, even those that don't need it. PDFs generated directly from software, like invoices or reports, already contain selectable text. Running OCR on these 'born-digital' documents is an unnecessary step that adds cost, processing time, and the potential for errors.

PDF4me has introduced a new endpoint designed to address this inefficiency. It allows users to directly extract text from digitally native PDFs using regular expressions (regex), completely skipping the OCR process when the text layer is already present and searchable.

This approach optimizes performance by avoiding redundant processing. Instead of converting pixels back into text, the endpoint reads the existing text layer. This is particularly beneficial for business automation workflows dealing with system-generated documents, exports, and contracts originating from sources like Microsoft Word.

The process is streamlined: users write a single regex pattern, specify the relevant pages, and send the request. The output is a simple JSON array of matched strings, without the overhead of per-match position data or complex labels, making it ideal for straightforward data extraction needs.

This 'Extract Text by Expression' endpoint is positioned as a lower-level tool compared to PDF4me's more sophisticated 'Parse Document' feature, which uses saved templates for complex, structured data extraction. The new endpoint is for simpler, pattern-based extraction tasks.

A working Python sample is available in PDF4me's MIT-licensed repository, demonstrating the core request/poll cycle. It highlights the importance of handling asynchronous responses and advises against disabling TLS certificate verification in production code.

headline_marked: NASA calls off mission to [[rescue Swift gamma-ray observatory]]
headline: NASA calls off mission to rescue Swift gamma-ray observatory
summary: A robotic mission to boost the Swift telescope's orbit has been abandoned due to technical issues with the rescue satellite.
details: NASA and Katalyst Space Technologies have announced the cancellation of a mission to rescue the Swift gamma-ray telescope. The rescue satellite, Link, was intended to capture Swift and boost its orbit to prevent reentry into Earth's atmosphere.

Link encountered "ongoing attitude control issues" shortly after launch, preventing it from completing its primary objective. While the satellite is still functional, it will now focus on demonstrating its close-in navigation system.

The Swift observatory, nearly 22 years old, has significantly outlived its original two-year design life. Despite its age, it remains crucial for detecting and studying gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe.

The rescue mission was a high-risk, high-reward endeavor, with NASA awarding Katalyst a $30 million contract for the project. The tight nine-month timeline for building and launching Link forced engineers to accept technical risks.

Problems arose in late July when Link experienced attitude control issues, with two of its three reaction wheels failing. This left the satellite reliant on its low-impulse plasma thrusters for orientation control.

Katalyst CEO Ghonhee Lee stated that the company is proud of the milestones achieved and will use the lessons learned to develop a playbook for future satellite servicing missions. The company's rendezvous sensors and robotic arms are key technologies for this growing field.

Despite the mission's failure to save Swift, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman emphasized the value of taking smart risks. The effort has already strengthened America's space industry and advanced in-space servicing capabilities.
